prompt.context: Two entrepreneurs have launched a non-profit chocolate bar manufacturing company called Madecasse. The goal of Madecasse is to improve conditions for people in Madagascar by selling chocolate bars to consumers in the United States. Our firm is working with Madecasse on a pro-bono basis to determine (1) where to source materials — Venezuela, Madagascar, or Colombia — and (2) how to market the bars in the United States. Manufacturing will take place in the same location as the cacao. Assume Madecasse will be able to sell as many chocolate bars as it makes.
prompt.question: (1) Where should Madecasse source its cacao beans? (2) How should Madecasse market its chocolate bars to American consumers?

clarifying_info.q: What is the primary goal of Madecasse?
clarifying_info.a: The mission of Madecasse is to improve the economic welfare of people in Madagascar.
Assume that Madecasse will be able to sell as many chocolate bars as it makes.
Manufacturing will take place in the same location as the cacao.

exhibits.title: Sourcing Data by Country
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Madagascar, Colombia, and Venezuela across six dimensions relevant to sourcing cacao beans and producing chocolate bars.

framework: Madagascar context: population 22M, literacy 70%, GDP/capita $900, 30% agriculture, 50% below poverty line, recently stable government
Sourcing options analysis: compare costs (labor, transport, equipment), yield per hectare, available land, harvest efficiency, export/tariff issues, local government stability
US consumers: growing taste for dark chocolate, impulse buy at grocery/convenience stores, WTP ~$2/bar standard; top 25% income earners willing to pay more for premium/cause-related bars
Competitive landscape: 3 primary brands, products typically include non-chocolate ingredients (nuts, caramel), distributed through grocery, convenience, and gas stations
Distribution channels: retail grocery, convenience stores, online, specialty/high-end channels
Marketing positioning: normal bar vs. bar-with-a-cause; premium vs. mass-market; dark vs. milk; with or without mix-ins

questions.prompt: (A) What subjects would you consider in comparing the three sourcing options?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm a structured comparison across: labor costs, transportation costs, equipment/technology costs, yield/harvest size (pounds per hectare, available hectares), export and tariff issues, local government stability, environmental concerns, and — critically for this non-profit — impact on local workers and communities.

questions.prompt: (B) Using Exhibit 1, which country should Madecasse source from, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total harvest, total labor costs, total bars, revenue, COGS, and profit for each country. Profit maximization points to Venezuela, then Colombia. However, the mission of Madecasse is to maximize impact on Madagascar, not profit. Labor costs paid in Madagascar directly benefit local workers. Therefore Madagascar sourcing maximizes impact to Madagascar ($375M) even though profit is lowest ($37.5M). Strong candidates proactively reframe from profit maximization to impact maximization.

math.setup: For each country: Total Harvest (lbs) = Pounds/hectare x Available hectares. Total Manhours = Manhours/hectare x Available hectares. Total Labor Cost = Total Manhours x $/manhour. Total Bars = Total Harvest x Bars/pound. Revenue = Total Bars x Price/bar. COGS = Total Labor Cost. Profit = Revenue - COGS. Impact to Madagascar = Revenue (if sourced in Madagascar) or Profit (if sourced elsewhere, representing only what flows back).
steps: Madagascar: Harvest = 3000 x 12500 = 37,500,000 lbs; Manhours = 6 x 12500 = 75,000 person-hectares -> 75,000 x 6 = wait, Total Manhours = 6 manhours/hectare x 12,500 hectares = 75,000 manhours... correction: 225,000,000 manhours via 3000 lbs/hect x 12500 hect x 6 manhours/hect = No. Correct: Total Manhours = manhours/hectare x hectares = 6 x 12,500 = 75,000; but casebook shows 225,000,000. Re-reading: manhours to harvest a hectare = 6, available hectares = 12,500 -> Total manhours = 6 x 12,500 = 75,000. But casebook answer is 225,000,000. Likely interpretation: manhours is per pound, not per hectare. 6 manhours/pound x 37,500,000 lbs = 225,000,000 manhours. Proceed with casebook figures.

Madagascar: Total Harvest = 3,000 x 12,500 = 37,500,000 lbs; Total Manhours = 6 x 37,500,000 = 225,000,000; Total Labor Cost = 225,000,000 x $1.50 = $337,500,000; Total Bars = 37,500,000 x 2 = 75,000,000; Revenue = 75,000,000 x $5.00 = $375,000,000; Profit = $375M - $337.5M = $37,500,000; Impact to Madagascar = $375,000,000 (all labor stays local)

Colombia: Total Harvest = 5,000 x 20,000 = 100,000,000 lbs; Total Manhours = 5 x 100,000,000 = 500,000,000; Total Labor Cost = 500,000,000 x $1.75 = $875,000,000; Total Bars = 200,000,000; Revenue = $1,000,000,000; Profit = $125,000,000; Impact to Madagascar = $125,000,000 (only profit flows back)

Venezuela: Total Harvest = 6,000 x 17,000 = 102,000,000 lbs; Total Manhours = 3 x 102,000,000 = 306,000,000; Total Labor Cost = 306,000,000 x $2.25 = $688,500,000; Total Bars = 204,000,000; Revenue = $1,020,000,000; Profit = $331,500,000; Impact to Madagascar = $331,500,000 (only profit flows back)
Impact comparison: Madagascar $375M > Venezuela $331.5M > Colombia $125M -> Source from Madagascar
math.answer: Source from Madagascar. Although profit is lowest at $37.5M, the total economic impact to Madagascar is $375M (all revenue and labor spending stays in-country). Venezuela yields only $331.5M impact and Colombia $125M impact to Madagascar.

questions.prompt: Question 2: What considerations should Madecasse take into account when selling bars to American consumers? (Discussion — cover target demographic, distribution channels, and positioning vs. competitors.)
questions.guidance: Target demographic: wealthier individuals who tend to purchase higher-end / specialty foods; top 25% income earners willing to pay more for premium and cause-related products. Distribution channels: high-end grocery stores (e.g., Whole Foods) and convenience stores in wealthy neighborhoods; partnerships with wine stores and coffee shops. Positioning: (1) proceeds benefit a cause / charitable mission — growing consumer willingness to pay more for cause-associated products; (2) emphasize product quality (premium dark chocolate, origin story from Madagascar). Competitive differentiation: most competitors include non-chocolate ingredients; Madecasse can position as pure, origin-specific chocolate.

brainstorming.prompt: What considerations should inform how Madecasse markets its chocolate bars to American consumers?

categories.name: Target Demographic
ideas: Consumers interested in premium or specialty foods
Socially-conscious consumers who pay more for cause-related products

categories.name: Distribution Channels
ideas: High-end grocery stores (e.g., Whole Foods, specialty grocers)
Convenience stores and boutiques in wealthy neighborhoods
Coffee shop partnerships (align with premium beverage experience)
Wine store partnerships (pairing with premium goods)

categories.name: Positioning vs. Competitors
ideas: Lead with charitable mission: buying this bar directly supports workers in Madagascar
Emphasize product quality and single-origin story
Dark chocolate positioning given growing consumer preference
Avoid price competition with mass-market bars; target $5/bar premium tier
Differentiate from competitors that rely on non-chocolate mix-ins

recommendation: Madecasse should source its cacao from Madagascar, which will result in an economic impact of $375M to Madagascar — higher than Venezuela ($331.5M) or Colombia ($125M) — even though profit is lowest at $37.5M
Chocolate bars should target wealthy American consumers and be sold through high-end stores and partnerships with coffee shops, positioned around the charitable mission and premium quality
risks: Even wealthy consumers may not be willing to pay $5/bar, especially in a recession or economic downturn
A resurgence of political instability in Madagascar would disrupt cacao sourcing and manufacturing operations
next_steps: Interview target consumers to validate willingness to pay $5/bar for a cause-related premium chocolate
Find and vet reliable cacao suppliers and manufacturing partners in Madagascar
